subject: Health and Human Development
name: Health and Human Development, Units 3 and 4
about: VCE, Australia's health and global health
syllabus: VCE Health and Human Development Study Design (from 2025), Units 3 and 4

units.title: Unit 3: Australia's health in a globalised world

points.title: Health, wellbeing and illness
points.brief: Health and wellbeing have physical, social, emotional, mental and spiritual dimensions, and illness is a person's experience of being unwell. All are dynamic and subjective.

points.title: Health as a resource
points.brief: Good health is a resource for individuals, communities, Australia and the world, because it lets people work, learn and take part.

points.title: Health status indicators
points.brief: Measures such as life expectancy, mortality, morbidity and self-assessed health status describe a population's health.

points.title: Incidence and prevalence
points.brief: Incidence counts new cases in a period; prevalence counts all cases at a time. Morbidity is how much illness there is.

points.title: Mortality and self-assessed health
points.brief: Maternal, infant and under-five mortality rates and how people rate their own health add to the picture of health status.

points.title: Burden of disease
points.brief: A measure of the impact of illness, injury and early death, counted in DALYs (disability-adjusted life years).

points.title: Years of life lost and years lived with disability
points.brief: A DALY is the sum of YLL (years lost to early death) and YLD (years lived with illness or disability).

points.title: Health-adjusted life expectancy
points.brief: HALE is the years a person can expect to live in full health, which is less than life expectancy.

points.title: Australia's health status
points.brief: Australia has one of the highest life expectancies in the world, with cancers, heart disease and mental health conditions leading the burden of disease.

points.title: Variations in health between groups
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, people in rural areas and people on low incomes have poorer health than other Australians.

points.title: Smoking, vaping and alcohol
points.brief: Tobacco, vaping and alcohol add to Australia's burden of disease through cancers, heart disease and injury.

points.title: Overweight and obesity
points.brief: Excess body weight raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease and some cancers.

points.title: Nutritional imbalance
points.brief: Eating too little fruit, vegetables, dairy and fibre and too much fat, salt and sugar harms Australians' health.

points.title: Old public health
points.brief: Early government action to improve health through the physical environment, such as clean water, sewerage and safe housing.

points.title: The biomedical approach
points.brief: Treating disease once it occurs, using doctors, technology and medicine. It saves lives but is costly and does not prevent illness.

points.title: The social model of health
points.brief: An approach that addresses the social, economic and environmental causes of health, involving communities and reducing inequity.

points.title: The Ottawa Charter
points.brief: The WHO's framework for health promotion, with five action areas and the strategies enable, mediate and advocate.

points.title: The five action areas
points.brief: Build healthy public policy, create supportive environments, strengthen community action, develop personal skills and reorient health services.

points.title: Health promotion
points.brief: Health promotion helps people gain control over their health, as Australia's mix of taxes, plain packaging and campaigns against smoking shows.

points.title: Improving Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health
points.brief: Programs led by community-controlled health organisations, which respect culture and self-determination, improve health and promote social justice.

points.title: Initiatives for healthy eating
points.brief: The Australian Dietary Guidelines, the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Guide to Healthy Eating promote better diets.

points.title: Challenges to changing diets
points.brief: Culture, habits, cost, food environments and food marketing make lasting changes to what people eat hard.

points.title: Australia's health system and equity
points.brief: Medicare, the PBS, the NDIS and private health insurance aim to give all Australians access to care, though gaps remain.

points.title: The National Disability Insurance Scheme
points.brief: The NDIS funds support for Australians with a permanent and significant disability, to help them live more independently.

units.title: Unit 4: Health and human development in a global context

points.title: Human development
points.brief: Human development means creating conditions where people can reach their potential, lead productive lives and have choices.

points.title: The Human Development Index
points.brief: The HDI combines life expectancy, education and income per person into one measure of a country's development.

points.title: Low-, middle- and high-income countries
points.brief: Countries differ in income, health care, education, infrastructure and life expectancy across these groups.

points.title: Health status across countries
points.brief: Life expectancy, child mortality and causes of death differ widely between high-income and low- and middle-income countries.

points.title: Sustainability and health
points.brief: Environmental, social and economic sustainability let health and human development last for future generations.

points.title: Safe water and sanitation
points.brief: Lack of clean water and toilets spreads disease such as diarrhoea, a leading cause of child deaths in poorer countries.

points.title: Poverty
points.brief: Poverty limits access to food, housing, health care and education, which lowers health and development.

points.title: Discrimination and health
points.brief: Discrimination by gender, ethnicity or disability can block access to education, work and health care.

points.title: Climate change and health
points.brief: Rising temperatures, extreme weather and changing disease patterns threaten health, hitting poorer countries hardest.

points.title: Conflict and migration
points.brief: War and forced migration destroy health systems, food supplies and shelter, and expose people to violence and disease.

points.title: World trade and health
points.brief: Global trade spreads the marketing of tobacco, e-cigarettes and processed foods, raising chronic disease in many countries.

points.title: Tourism and health
points.brief: Tourism brings income and jobs but can spread disease and strain local resources.

points.title: Digital technologies and health
points.brief: Digital technology spreads health information, telehealth and education, but access is uneven between and within countries.

points.title: What the SDGs are
points.brief: Seventeen goals agreed by United Nations members in 2015 to end poverty, protect the planet and improve lives by 2030.

points.title: SDG 3 and its targets
points.brief: Goal 3 aims to ensure healthy lives and wellbeing for all at all ages, with targets on child and maternal deaths and disease.

points.title: Links between SDG 3 and other goals
points.brief: Progress on SDG 3 depends on ending poverty and hunger, education, gender equality, clean water and responsible consumption (SDGs 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 and 12).

points.title: The goal and objectives of the WHO
points.brief: The WHO aims for the highest possible health for everyone, working on universal health coverage, health emergencies and healthier populations.

points.title: Types of aid
points.brief: Bilateral aid goes from one government to another, multilateral aid through bodies such as the UN, and non-government organisations give humanitarian and development aid.

points.title: Australia's aid program
points.brief: Australia gives aid through the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, mostly to countries in the Indo-Pacific.

points.title: Non-government organisations
points.brief: Groups such as charities run health and development programs, often working closely with local communities.

points.title: What makes a program work
points.brief: Programs work best when they are run with the community, target real needs, build local skills and can be sustained.

points.title: Evaluating a health program
points.brief: A program is judged by whether it reached its goals, who it helped, whether it lasts and its links to the SDGs.

points.title: Taking action for global health
points.brief: Individuals can volunteer, fundraise, advocate or make ethical choices to support health and human development.
